analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional redistricting away from politicians and gives it to an independent commission.
analysis.headline: The redistricting bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the House, where one Democrat introduced it and two committees held it until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a 14-member independent commission to draw every state's congressional district map after the 2020 census, instead of letting state politicians do it. The commission would be barred from considering incumbents' homes or voters' party leanings, and would have to work in public with a website posting its drafts, data, and votes. Congress would then have to vote on the commission's maps through a fast-track process with no amendments.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters. Today, the politicians who run state government draw the congressional map in nearly every state, and the people who draw the lines can choose their voters — protecting incumbents and the majority party. This bill would hand that job to a commission barred from considering where incumbents live or how districts have voted in the past, required to keep counties, cities, and neighborhoods together where possible, and required to conduct all of its work in public with a chance for citizens to comment on every draft map.

how_it_helps.text: The commission may not consider the voting history of a district, the party affiliation of its residents, or the home addresses of incumbent members of Congress when drawing maps, except where the Voting Rights Act requires otherwise.

Commission meetings and hearings would be open to the public, and the commission would have to post every proposed map, the underlying census and election data, its recorded votes, and transcripts of its hearings on a public website, with a 14-day public comment period before voting on a final plan.

The commission's map criteria require districts to keep counties, municipalities, and neighborhoods together where practicable, to be compact and contiguous, and to be as equal in population as mathematically possible.

Once the commission approves plans for all states, Congress must consider the enabling bill on a fast-track schedule with no amendments allowed, making it difficult to quietly dilute or block the maps.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the politicians who control state legislatures would lose their power to draw their own district lines. Taxpayers would fund the commission, whose members are paid at a senior federal pay rate for each day worked and who may hire a staff director plus up to five staff each, with amounts authorized as necessary.

drawbacks.text: The commission's 14 members are appointed by the four congressional party leaders — the Speaker, the House minority leader, and the Senate majority and minority leaders — with up to 7 from one party, so the same political leadership that benefits from gerrymandering would choose the map-drawers.

The bill moves a decision currently made by each state's government to a federal commission and a mandatory vote of Congress, a shift of power away from states that critics of federal redistricting mandates have long objected to.
The fast-track process allows only limited debate in the House (2 hours) and Senate (100 hours total) and bars all amendments, trading transparency of procedure for speed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Removing the conflict of interest in which elected officials draw the districts that determine whether they keep their jobs is a real gain for voters, and the bill's transparency requirements are unusually detailed. The main weakness is design: the party leaders who profit from current maps appoint the commission, and a federal commission overriding state map-drawing raises a genuine structural objection. On balance, the bill addresses a self-serving system with a workable, if imperfect, alternative.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Rules Committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Judiciary subcommittee two weeks later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Blumenauer introduced the bill on January 31, 2012, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Rules Committee.
On February 16, 2012, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution, which was the last recorded action on the bill.
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the state politicians who control redistricting kept their power to draw congressional maps to their own advantage, and the party leadership that appoints map-drawers faced no competing commission. Voters gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents who kept their map-drawing power

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Commission for Independent Redistricting Act and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and members of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on the Constitution; no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill was ever scheduled.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee calendars, 112th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; it received no floor action of any kind during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat introduced the bill and not a single member of either party — Republican or Democratic — cosponsored it, in a House controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill strips incumbents of the decisive advantage that the people who draw congressional maps may not consider where they live, and bars the map-drawers from using past voting patterns that favor them. Their interest in keeping that power runs directly against voters' interest in competitive, fairly drawn districts.

industries.industry: State legislatures and their majority parties
industries.note: State politicians currently draw most congressional maps, and the party that controls a statehouse can entrench its House delegation for a decade. The bill would transfer that job to an independent commission after the 2020 census.

industries.industry: Congressional party leaders (Speaker, House and Senate minority and majority leaders)
industries.note: The bill takes away the maps but keeps the appointments: the four congressional party leaders would name all 14 commissioners, up to 7 of them from one party. Their institutional power over House delegations would be mediated, not eliminated.
